title: The Temple (1 Kings 8)
hookLine: the heaven of heavens can't contain God, yet he chooses to dwell

lines: THE ARK INTO THE HOLY OF HOLIES.
cards: Seven years of building. Cedar from Lebanon, stone cut at the quarry so no hammer is heard on the site, gold over the inner walls. Solomon has built a house for God in Jerusalem, on the hill above his father's city.
Dedication day. The priests carry the ark of the covenant, the same ark David danced before, into the innermost room, the Holy of Holies, and set it under the wings of the cherubim.
They step back out, and a cloud fills the house, so thick the priests can't stand to do their work. The text says the glory of the Lord had filled the house.

teach.b: Solomon stands before the altar in front of the whole assembly, spreads his hands toward heaven, and prays. On the proudest day of his reign, he undercuts his own building.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Is it then to be thought that God should indeed dwell upon earth? for if heaven, and the heavens of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house which I have built?"
No building can hold God. So what is the Temple for?

teach.h: A PLACE WHERE GOD WILL HEAR.
teach.b: Solomon answers in the rest of the prayer: so that God's eyes may be open on this house night and day, and God will hear whoever prays toward it.
The sick, the guilty, the soldier far away, even the foreigner from a distant land. The Temple isn't a box for God. It's a place God chooses, freely, to be found.
He can't be contained, and still he chooses to dwell. Catholics see that choice taken further.
John's Gospel says the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and Jesus calls his own body a temple. Saint Paul tells Christians they themselves are God's temple.
And in Catholic churches there's a tabernacle, often with a lamp burning beside it, where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, because Catholics believe Christ is truly present there.

teach.h: THE HEAVENS OF HEAVENS CANNOT CONTAIN THEE.
teach.b: People kneel or genuflect as they pass. Solomon's question still stands: can God really dwell on earth? The Catholic answer is yes: not because anyone built something big enough, but because, Catholics say, he chooses to.

how: Catholic churches keep the Blessed Sacrament in a tabernacle, usually with a sanctuary lamp burning nearby, and Catholics genuflect toward it; the Church also keeps feasts for the dedication of churches, including the Lateran Basilica in Rome.

o: Solomon's house for God, filled with a cloud
the movable tent where Israel kept the ark
the royal palace Solomon built for himself

p: filled the house; priests couldn't stand
where Catholics keep the Blessed Sacrament

s: Solomon thought God could live inside the Temple
he said the heaven of heavens can't contain God, how much less this house.
Solomon's prayer includes foreigners who come to pray
he asks God to hear the stranger from a far country too.
the priests finished the ceremony as planned
a cloud filled the house, and they couldn't stand to minister.

games.q: you're Solomon. you've spent seven years building the finest house in the land for God, and today you dedicate it before all Israel. what do you say?
o: now God lives here, with us.
even heaven can't contain you, how much less this house.
games.why: at the height of his triumph, Solomon admits no building can hold God, and asks only that God hear the prayers made toward it.

practice: Pick one small spot near you, a windowsill, a bedside table, and picture what could mark it as a place to stop: a candle, a cross, a picture of someone you love, or an empty space kept clear on purpose.
Solomon knew size wasn't the point. If you pray, ask God to meet you there; if you don't, let it be a place you come back to yourself.

wordCard.voice: The Temple. The house Solomon built in Jerusalem, filled with God's glory, which he knew could never contain God, a place God chose to be found. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: house. The Temple is called the house of the Lord; the same word means a family, a dynasty, a home.

carryVoice: Your line: he chooses to dwell. No house could ever hold him. See you tomorrow.
